overview: This file concerns proposals during the Allied occupation to change Japan from left-hand to right-hand road traffic. It begins with a State Department memorandum compiling the side of the road used throughout the world, followed by an inquiry into whether General MacArthur and the U.S. Army had considered changing Japan’s system. An outgoing airgram then asks the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo for a fuller assessment, and duplicated incoming copies explain that a 1946 Eighth Army proposal had been rejected because of conversion costs, disruption to streetcars and buses, Japanese objections, anticipated British opposition in Allied bodies, legal concerns about altering local customs under occupation, and the priority placed on economic stabilization. Despite the broader file title, the surviving documents deal almost entirely with automobile traffic rules rather than carrier pigeons or bus-line regulation generally.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on driving sides in selected countries
subfiles.about: Provides a worldwide country-by-country compilation showing whether road traffic keeps to the right or left.
subfiles.summary: Whitmack reports a table of countries' driving sides compiled from the Auto Association and embassies, listing Japan as left-driving, framing the later discussion of changing Japan's traffic rule.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the “Rule of the Road” in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports preliminary findings on whether the U.S. Army had considered changing Japan to right-hand traffic.
subfiles.summary: Hulick finds no Pentagon file on changing Japan's traffic rule; MacArthur considered it in 1945 but dropped it as impractical given streetcar conversion costs.

subfiles.title: Outgoing airgram A-8 requesting a study of changing Japan’s traffic direction
subfiles.from: Department of State; Robert A. Lovett, Acting
subfiles.about: Requests a detailed assessment of whether the occupation offers a practical opportunity to change Japan from left-hand to right-hand traffic.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-8 argues occupation and American vehicles make converting Japan to right-hand driving unusually feasible despite high streetcar-conversion costs, asking Tokyo to assess renewed action before the 1949 UN road-traffic conference.

subfiles.title: Tokyo airgram A-29 on the rejected traffic change proposal, retrieved copy
subfiles.about: Reconstructs the 1946 proposal to introduce right-hand traffic in Japan and explains why occupation authorities rejected it.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-29 reports the Eighth Army's 1946 conversion proposal, backed by a GHQ study given American-vehicle dominance, was rejected over huge costs, Japanese opposition, anticipated British resistance, and occupation-law concerns, becoming a dead issue.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for Tokyo airgram A-29
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Designates an attached copy of Tokyo airgram A-29 as the record copy replacing an unreturned original action copy.
subfiles.summary: Record-copy form documents replacing the missing original action copy for Tokyo airgram A-29, filed at 894.7971/2-849.

subfiles.title: Tokyo airgram A-29 on the rejected traffic change proposal, received copy
subfiles.about: Provides a received duplicate of Tokyo’s detailed history and assessment of the proposed switch to right-hand traffic in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Received copy repeats the Eighth Army's 1946 traffic-conversion proposal, revised cost estimates (¥100M to ¥84M), Japanese opposition, predicted British resistance, and occupation-law concerns, confirming rejection unless financing could be found.

interest: Shows postwar study of switching Japan to right-hand traffic, rejected as too costly amid occupation and Allied politics.
